source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo shows a human-like decline on verbal n-back as n goes 1 to 3. Capacity is about 3 items in base, feedback and CoT variants. Noise (distractors) lowers capacity.
numbers: Temperature 1; 50 blocks of letter sequences per condition; metric d-prime. d' falls to about 1 at n=3 in all verbal variants except noise.
quote: its capacity limit is similar to that of humans
limits: n=3 is below Miller 7 and near Cowan 4. Critiqued by Hu and Lewis as task misunderstanding.
agent_relevance: Do not read n-back failure as a hard memory limit; check task comprehension first.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Spatial n-back (3x3 grid) repeats the same decline, with lower capacity than verbal. CoT reasoning prompts significantly improved performance. An abstract spatial reasoning variant had much lower capacity.
numbers: Variants: base, noise, feedback, CoT, larger grid, abstract reasoning. Per-cell values only in figures.
limits: Authors attribute the spatial gap to higher difficulty.
agent_relevance: CoT externalises state and raises effective capacity: write state down.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Model comparison on verbal n-back base task: GPT-4 above GPT-3.5. Six open models (Bloomz-7B, Bloomz-7B1-mt, ChatGLM-6B v1.0 and v1.1, Vicuna-7B and 13B) have very low capacity, nearly indistinguishable.
numbers: GPT-4 not tested for n>3 because of API cost, so its exact limit is unknown.
limits: Weak models may fail from task misunderstanding (Hu and Lewis), not capacity.
agent_relevance: Capacity measures on small models are confounded with instruction following.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
finding: Small decoder-only transformers trained from scratch on N-back lose accuracy as N rises. Test accuracy declines logarithmically with N out to N=6. Larger models (more layers or heads) stay above 95% but still dip slightly.
numbers: 1-layer 1-head model: Kruskal-Wallis H=38.517, p<.001, eta-squared 0.248. Sizes tested: layers 1-2, heads 1,2,4.
limits: Decline is smooth, not a cliff at 7. Toy models, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: The limit is gradual and architecture-linked; there is no sharp magic number.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
finding: Mechanism claim: the attention score at position i-N rises with accuracy during training. Total entropy of the attention matrix increases with N and is negatively correlated with accuracy, so dispersed attention may cause the limit.
numbers: Correlational; one-layer one-head focus; no causal test in real LLMs.
quote: dispersion of attention scores might be the cause of the capacity limit
limits: Fits executive-attention theory, not a store-size theory.
agent_relevance: Capacity limit is about attention dilution; fewer, focused items in context help.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? N-back
finding: Weak models' n-back errors match a different m-back task (m not equal n). They misunderstand or drift even with instructions and demos. GPT-3.5 starts with the right task and drifts as errors accumulate.
numbers: Score table for 1/2/3-back (read from layout): Llama 3.1 8B 1.00/0.14/0.17; GPT-3.5 Turbo 1.00/0.51/0.43; Llama 3.1 70B 1.00/0.99/0.93.
quote: poor performance is due at least in part to a limitation in task comprehension
limits: Failed-interpretation critique of the Gong claim. Task-set maintenance is itself a working-memory-like demand.
agent_relevance: Restate the task rule in the prompt each turn to avoid task drift.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? N-back
finding: The best open model (Llama 3.1 70B Instruct) handles n-back far beyond 3, up to 10-back.
numbers: Task accuracy 90.08%, 90.08%, 84.75% for n=8,9,10; retrieval accuracy 79.83%, 80.17%, 71.67% for the same n.
limits: Shows no hard capacity of 3 in strong LLMs. Limits depend on model and prompting.
agent_relevance: Storage fidelity is high in strong models; the bottleneck is manipulation.

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? N-back
finding: Attention analysis: Qwen 1.5 14B has a head whose attention matches the needed retrieval (max 71.98% at one layer and head). Llama 3.1 8B and 70B are far more diffuse (max 4.86% and 8.52%).
numbers: Metric MRAT; single-trial examples.
limits: Mixed support for the attention-dispersion story of Gong and Zhang.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one mechanism for all models.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: Simple span: LLMs recall up to 50 digits forward perfectly but falter at about 15 backward. Reversal (a manipulation) breaks recall. Far above the human span of 7.
numbers: Many frontier and open models; forward span tested to 50, backward degrades from about 15.
limits: Storage is cheap, manipulation is costly. Matches Baddeley's storage versus executive split.
agent_relevance: Plan around manipulation load: write steps out instead of reordering mentally.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: Reasoning models do not consistently improve working memory spans (backward digit span, reading span). They help weak baselines (Llama-8B, Qwen-8B) but stay below ceiling. Many errors come from thought strings that loop without converging or hallucinate.
numbers: Reasoning versus instruct variants compared on backward span and reading span.
limits: Reasoning tokens act as a central executive only partly.
agent_relevance: Long thinking does not cure span limits; keep chains short and checked.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: Executive Functioning in LLMs
finding: LLMs beat human norms on most WM tasks but fall below humans on executive tasks. More WM capacity did not correlate with better executive or problem-solving scores. Flanker accuracy 40-60% versus human 93-96%.
numbers: Tasks: n-back, digit spans, operation span, reading span, flanker, set shifting.
limits: Attention control and inhibition are the weak parts, not capacity.
agent_relevance: Spend scaffold effort on inhibition and shifting checks, not on capacity tricks.

source: Huang et al. (2026) On the Failure of Latent State Persistence in LLMs
finding: LLMs fail to track a hidden number through updates when it is not written in context. Externalising state with CoT or reasoning models partly fixes it, except GPT-4o.
numbers: Invariant success under CoT: GPT-4o-mini 5/150 (3.3%), GPT-4o 2024-05-13 26/150 (17.3%), GPT-4o 2024-08-06 31/150 (20.7%); text reports 10-30% gains with CoT.
limits: Tests unexpressed state, a stricter demand than span.
agent_relevance: Write all state into context. Never rely on silent internal state.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs
finding: Proactive interference test (PI-LLM): retrieval of the latest key value falls log-linearly toward zero as stale updates accumulate, though the answer sits just before the query.
numbers: Updates per key 3 to 400 (log-spaced); 46 keys; dozens of models. At 400 updates the mid-size group drops to 0% with one exception; large models stay high.
quote: accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as interference accumulates
limits: Human PI resilience tracks WM capacity. It is not a context-length effect.
agent_relevance: Prune stale or superseded facts from context; do not just append.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs
finding: With strictly sequential updates, accuracy stays near perfect until a model-specific threshold, then drops abruptly to near zero: a step, which the authors read as a hard capacity limit. Larger models have a higher threshold.
numbers: Contrasts with the gradual log-linear decay under shuffled order.
limits: Ordering changes the shape: capacity cliff versus graded decay.
agent_relevance: Group related updates contiguously and summarise them.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs
finding: Interference Endurance Score (area under accuracy-vs-interference curve) is predicted by parameter count, not by context window size. Telling the model to forget or ignore earlier input helps little.
numbers: Regression: parameter count significant, t=3.03, p=0.005, N=30 models; combined model explains 26.1% of variance.
limits: Only marginal gains from strategic-forgetting prompts.
agent_relevance: Prompting cannot erase stale items; remove them from the context instead.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Multi-document QA accuracy is U-shaped by answer position: best at start or end, worst in the middle. GPT-3.5-Turbo can drop by more than 20% in the worst case, even below closed-book accuracy.
numbers: Closed-book 56.1% for GPT-3.5-Turbo, oracle 88.3%; Claude-1.3 closed-book 48.3%, oracle 76.1%; 20-document setting.
limits: Serial position curve like human primacy and recency.
agent_relevance: Put key items at the start and end of the prompt; keep contexts short.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Key-value retrieval: query-aware contextualization (query before and after data) makes GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) perfect at 300 pairs; without it the worst case is 45.6%. Extra retrieved documents add little (1.5% GPT-3.5, 1% Claude).
numbers: Synthetic KV task; 300 key-value pairs.
limits: A simple scaffold gives a large effect on a capacity-style task.
agent_relevance: Repeat the question before and after long material.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?
finding: All 17 models claim 32K+ context but only about half keep satisfactory performance at 32K. Multi-hop tracing and aggregation degrade fastest.
numbers: Gemini-1.5-Pro 95.9 at 32K and 94.4 at 128K; GPT-4 93.2 at 32K, 81.2 at 128K (effective 64K); Llama3.1 70B 94.8 at 32K, 66.6 at 128K; Mistral-v0.2 7B 75.4 at 32K, 13.8 at 128K; DBRX 63.1 at 32K, 2.4 at 64K.
limits: Effective capacity is far below nominal capacity and falls with task complexity.
agent_relevance: Budget by effective, not claimed, context; test task type, not just retrieval.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
finding: Agent loop with a small main context (system prompt, read-write working context, FIFO queue with a recursive summary of evicted messages) plus external archival and recall storage. The model pages data in and out via function calls. Framed as virtual memory, not as Miller chunking.
numbers: Deep memory retrieval accuracy: GPT-3.5 38.7% to 66.9%, GPT-4 32.1% to 92.5%, GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% to 93.4% with MemGPT.
limits: OS paging, not chunking; the recursive summary is a form of compression.
agent_relevance: Working-context block plus eviction summary is a ready template for our scaffold.

source: Upadhayay et al. (2024) Cognitive Overload Attack: Prompt Injection for Long Context
finding: Applies cognitive load theory. Stacking 1 to 6 irrelevant tasks degrades answers on an observation task. Overloaded prompts then jailbreak models, so overload is an attack surface.
numbers: Attack success rate (Forbidden Questions): Claude-3-Opus 99.99%, Llama-3-70B 92.67%, GPT-4 90.95%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 84.05%, Gemini-1.0-Pro 75.43%. JailbreakBench: Claude-3-Opus 97%, GPT-4 90%.
limits: Scored by LLM judges; an attack paper, not a capacity measure.
agent_relevance: Overloaded steps weaken checks; keep each step to one demand.

source: Hu et al. (2024) HiAgent: Hierarchical Working Memory Management for Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
finding: Direct use of chunking in an agent loop. The LLM sets a subgoal, acts, then replaces that subgoal's action-observation pairs with a summary (a chunk), keeping detail only for the current subgoal. Cites Miller 1956.
numbers: AgentBoard, 5 tasks: success rate 42 vs 21 (twofold); progress rate +23.94%; steps -3.8; context length -35.02%; run time -19.42%. Ablation against subgoals without trimming: success +20%.
quote: leverages subgoals as memory chunks to manage the working memory
limits: Closest operational use of Miller chunking in LLM agents. Gripper progress rate slipped 1.5%.
agent_relevance: Subgoal chunking with summaries is a strong candidate operator.

source: Lee et al. (2024) ReadAgent: A Human-Inspired Reading Agent with Gist Memory of Very Long Contexts
finding: Three steps: pagination (LLM picks episode breaks), gisting (compress pages), lookup (re-read pages when needed). Extends effective context 3.5x to 20x.
numbers: NarrativeQA Gutenberg: +12.97% LLM rating and +31.98% ROUGE-L over best retrieval, 20x context. QuALITY: gist compression 85.53%; one-page lookup 76.00%; six-page ReadAgent-P 64.75%; ReadAgent-S 58.53%; 3.5x context with 20.4% fewer words.
limits: More lookups mean a smaller compression rate; gist memory is still bounded by context length.
agent_relevance: Chunk, gist, then selectively re-expand supports long tasks.

source: Gobet and Lane, CHREST (Wikipedia summary)
finding: CHREST is a symbolic chunking architecture (successor to EPAM) with limited attention and STM. Chunks sit in a discrimination network and grow into templates. It simulates chess recall from novice to master and child language.
numbers: Visual STM capacity set to 3 chunks. The page gives no fit statistics.
limits: Secondary source; fits not checked against primary papers.
agent_relevance: Template slots over chunks hint at how a schema could compress familiar situations.

source: Soar chunking (Wikipedia summary)
finding: Soar chunking: impasse, substate, resolution, then compile the substate reasoning into a new rule. Later similar cases fire directly with no impasse, so deliberate reasoning becomes reactive.
numbers: R1-Soar, Tower of Hanoi, Eight Puzzle, scheduling. One operator cycle is about 50 ms. No chunking-specific figures.
limits: A chunk here is a learned rule, not a Miller item count.
agent_relevance: Cache solved sub-problems as reusable rules or schemas.

source: Search gap note (this run)
finding: No LLM study located that directly tests Miller's 7 plus or minus 2 or spontaneous chunk formation. Found studies test n-back, spans, interference and context use. Only agent papers (HiAgent, ReadAgent) use chunking as a method.
numbers: arXiv and OpenAlex APIs returned nothing and the WebSearch budget ran out. Zhang et al. (EMNLP 2024, working memory limits) not opened; Xu et al. (NAACL 2024 cognitive overload) downloaded but not read.
limits: Absence is not proof; coverage is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Treat the 7 plus or minus 2 analogy as metaphor; use measured effective-context curves instead.
